Reliance on electricity from a greener mill that turns to the use of renewable natural gas or even hydrogen in place of traditional natural gas was suggested. Those zero carbon fuels used in conjunction with the existing biofuels will aid in reducing the carbon impact of RF and US. To gain insight into the energy inputs for paper drying, a forward-looking analysis was conducted on existing fuel mix contributions. Table 13 gives the fuel mix with the energy consumption (TBtu) for the overall pulp and paper manufacturing process and the same mix has been assumed here for the conventional paper drying process. Table 14 presents data on fuel mix contributions from various sources spanning from 2002 to 2018, with extrapolations to 2024. These tables are based on data from the DOE Manufacturing Energy Consumption Survey (MECS). It's important to note that steam usage associated with conventional paper drying primarily originates from natural gas (Power Boiler) and biomass boilers (with a zero-carbon footprint). These carbon footprints will serve as the foundation for determining how to achieve a 25% reduction in carbon intensity. This approach aligns with Scope 2 considerations for carbon reduction, where the emphasis is on the impact of purchased energy rather than on-site energy use (Scope 1). The calculation of this 60% reduction is based on a reference value of 330 pounds per million British thermal units (lb/MMBtu) (or 1,125 lb/megawatt hour) for the Southeast U.S., as indicated in Table 15.
